narrative:
Your application was rejected because the model predicts a 99.2% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. This decision is based on how your academic profile compares to students who typically pass. The most critical factor is your undergraduate GPA, which at 2.90 is significantly lower than the average of 3.24 among successful students. Your LSAT score of 34 is also below the average of 37.27, and your school performance in both Year 1 and Year 3 placed you in the 2nd decile, far below the typical 6th decile of those who pass. While your family income being upper-middle class is common among successful applicants, and studying full-time is typical, these factors alone cannot overcome the academic gaps.

To understand what would change this outcome, we explored "what if" scenarios—minimal changes that would flip the prediction to "pass." Out of 10 such scenarios, every single one required a change in your undergraduate GPA. Specifically, your GPA would need to increase by an average of 0.1 points, from 2.90 to 3.00. No other factors—your school deciles, LSAT score, family income, or full-time status—changed in any scenario. This means the model sees your GPA as the single most impactful and adjustable factor for improving your chances.

The consistency of this finding is striking: your GPA was the only feature that changed in 100% of counterfactuals, while all other features remained the same. This tells us that even a small improvement in your GPA could be enough to shift the prediction from failure to success. Your current GPA of 2.90 is just below a critical threshold, and raising it to 3.00 appears to be the most direct path to approval.

For you personally, this means focusing on your undergraduate coursework is the most actionable step. Since your LSAT score and school deciles are already set, and your family income and study status are not factors that need changing, the clearest path forward is to improve your GPA. Even a modest increase of 0.1 points could make a decisive difference, bringing you closer to the average of students who pass. Consider retaking courses or seeking academic support to boost your grades, as this single change appears to be the key to flipping the model's prediction in your favor.
